bibl.title: Measuring Individual Differences in Generic Beliefs in Conspiracy Theories Across Cultures: Conspiracy Mentality Questionnaire

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: the GENERAL tendency to believe conspiracy theories, as something separable from belief in any particular one - and the problem of measuring it in a way that survives translation into another culture
span.quote: Individuals differ not only in the degree to which they believe in specific conspiracy theories, but also in their general susceptibility to explanations based on such theories, that is, their conspiracy mentality . We present the Conspiracy Mentality Questionnaire (CMQ), an instrument designed to efficiently assess differences in the generic tendency to engage in conspiracist ideation within and across cultures.

span.label: whether a five-item instrument with no named conspiracies in it can measure conspiracy mentality equivalently across European, North American and Middle Eastern samples
span.quote: In this context, we will propose the Conspiracy Mentality Questionnaire (CMQ), a short (5-item) measure of generic conspiracy beliefs that we administered in a large ( N = 7,766) international study spanning North American (US), Western European (UK and Ireland; Germany), and Middle Eastern (Turkey) cultures

span.label: the CMQ - five items, one dimension, three languages - with measurement equivalence tested across cultures, which the paper says none of the competing instruments had done
span.quote: Analyses based on a cross-cultural sample (Study 1a; N = 7,766) supported the conceptualization of conspiracy mentality as a one-dimensional construct across the three language versions of the CMQ that is stable across time (Study 1b; N = 141). Multi-group confirmatory factor analysis demonstrated cross-cultural measurement equivalence of the CMQ items.

span.label: method
span.quote: In this context, we will propose the Conspiracy Mentality Questionnaire (CMQ), a short (5-item) measure of generic conspiracy beliefs that we administered in a large ( N = 7,766) international study spanning North American (US), Western European (UK and Ireland; Germany), and Middle Eastern (Turkey) cultures

span.label: a stable individual disposition that predicts belief in conspiracy theories the believer has never heard of - INCLUDING MUTUALLY CONTRADICTORY ONES AND ONES INVENTED FOR AN EXPERIMENT
span.quote: In fact, this tendency even extends to beliefs in mutually contradictory conspiracy theories, and to beliefs in fully fictitious conspiracy theories. Thus, those who believe that Princess Diana faked her own death are also more likely to believe that she was murdered

span.label: four studies: a cross-cultural sample of 7,766 for factor structure and measurement equivalence, a retest of 141, and re-analyses of three datasets (total 476) for convergent, discriminant and predictive validity
span.term: four studies: a cross-cultural sample of 7,766 for factor structure and measurement equivalence, a retest of 141, and re-analyses of three datasets (total 476) for convergent, discriminant and predictive validity
span.quote: Analyses based on a cross-cultural sample (Study 1a; N = 7,766) supported the conceptualization of conspiracy mentality as a one-dimensional construct across the three language versions of the CMQ that is stable across time (Study 1b; N = 141). Multi-group confirmatory factor analysis demonstrated cross-cultural measurement equivalence of the CMQ items.

span.label: THE EVIDENCE THAT A GENERIC SCALE IS POSSIBLE AT ALL IS THE INCOHERENCE OF THE BELIEFS: `those who believe that Princess Diana FAKED HER OWN DEATH are also more likely to believe that SHE WAS MURDERED`. If contradictory theories rise together, what varies is not the content but the disposition
span.quote: In fact, this tendency even extends to beliefs in mutually contradictory conspiracy theories, and to beliefs in fully fictitious conspiracy theories. Thus, those who believe that Princess Diana faked her own death are also more likely to believe that she was murdered

span.label: and the same argument in its cleanest form: believers in a real conspiracy theory are more likely to endorse `A CONSPIRACY THEORY THAT WAS PURPOSELY DEVELOPED FOR A SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY STUDY`. The item has no referent in the world and it still loads
span.quote: those who believe in “real-world conspiracy theories” (i.e., that John F. Kennedy fell victim to an organized conspiracy) are more likely to believe that there was a conspiracy behind the success of the Red Bull energy drink – a conspiracy theory that was purposely developed for a social psychology study

span.label: THE PAPER'S OWN ORGANISING DISTINCTION IS DECLARED NOT CLEAR CUT, BY ITS AUTHORS, IN THE PAPER THAT RESTS ON IT: an instrument with items `not mentioning any actors or possible topics of conspiracies RUNS THE DANGER OF NOT ADEQUATELY CAPTURING THE CONSTRUCT ... the distinction between scales measuring GENERIC and SPECIFIC conspiracy beliefs IS NOT AS CLEAR CUT AS ONE MAY INITIALLY SUSPECT`
span.quote: Lastly, an instrument with items not mentioning any actors or possible topics of conspiracies runs the danger of not adequately capturing the construct. Thus, in our view, the distinction between scales measuring generic and specific conspiracy beliefs is not as clear cut as one may initially suspect.

span.label: and the five items are not content-free either: `our scale is NOT COMPLETELY FREE FROM CONTENT-RELATED ASPECTS`, with the government-monitoring item named as the offender - and it is exactly the item that `showed a comparatively LOW FACTOR LOADING IN THE TURKISH LANGUAGE VERSION`. THE CONTENT AND THE CROSS-CULTURAL FAILURE ARE THE SAME ITEM
span.quote: Second, we are aware of the fact that our scale is not completely free from content-related aspects. For example, the item “I think government agencies closely monitor all citizens” does provide more specific information than the item “I think that events which superficially seem to lack a connection are often the result of secret activities.” This difference may be responsible for the fact that the former item showed a comparatively low factor loading in the Turkish language version.

span.label: the samples were `NOT REPRESENTATIVE of the general population of the different countries`, and the paper asks that generalisation `proceed with caution`
span.quote: First, our samples were not representative of the general population of the different countries, and any generalization should therefore proceed with caution.

span.label: and the state of the field it is joining: of the two existing generic instruments, `NEITHER SCALE HAS BEEN VALIDATED IN NON-WESTERN CULTURES and so far NEITHER SCALE HAS BEEN ADOPTED BY RESEARCHERS OTHER THAN THE ORIGINAL AUTHORS`. Four instruments, no shared use
span.quote: Both the authors of the Generic Conspiracist Beliefs Scale and the Conspiracy Mentality Scale provide initial evidence for the convergent and discriminant validity of their instruments. However, neither scale has been validated in non-Western cultures and so far neither scale has been adopted by researchers other than the original authors.

span.label: the sample is dominated by one country and skewed male - most respondents are German and nearly twice as many men as women
span.quote: This resulted in a final sample of N = 7,673 participants (4,919 men, 2,694 women, 60 unreported) between the age of 18 and 67 years ( M = 29.1, SD = 10.2).

span.label: recruitment ran through the first author's prior participants and study-listing sites, then spread virally through social networks and media links, so who took part was not controlled
span.quote: Participants initially were recruited by solicitation e-mails to participants in prior online studies conducted by the first author and by posting the study on sites listing online studies (e.g., Reips and Lengler, 2005 ; Kathryn Gardner’s onlinepsychresearch.co.uk and John H.

span.label: the cross-cultural dimension is stated to have been largely absent from conspiracy research, with one named exception
span.quote: The cross-cultural dimension has so far been largely absent from research on conspiracy theories (for a notable exception examining the UK and Austria, see Swami et al., 2011 ).

span.label: measurement equivalence across the English, German and Turkish versions, by multi-group confirmatory factor analysis on 7,766 respondents
span.note: eliminates: language version as an explanation of between-country differences - which is what makes the absolute levels comparable at all · outcome: held
span.quote: Analyses based on a cross-cultural sample (Study 1a; N = 7,766) supported the conceptualization of conspiracy mentality as a one-dimensional construct across the three language versions of the CMQ that is stable across time (Study 1b; N = 141). Multi-group confirmatory factor analysis demonstrated cross-cultural measurement equivalence of the CMQ items.

span.label: whether a scale free of named conspiracies still measures the construct
span.note: eliminates: nothing, and the authors raise the objection themselves: such an instrument `RUNS THE DANGER OF NOT ADEQUATELY CAPTURING THE CONSTRUCT`, and the generic/specific distinction is `NOT AS CLEAR CUT AS ONE MAY INITIALLY SUSPECT` · outcome: failed
span.quote: Lastly, an instrument with items not mentioning any actors or possible topics of conspiracies runs the danger of not adequately capturing the construct. Thus, in our view, the distinction between scales measuring generic and specific conspiracy beliefs is not as clear cut as one may initially suspect.

span.label: convergent validity against another validated generic measure, and predictive validity for specific beliefs while controlling a broad set of individual differences
span.note: eliminates: the objection that the CMQ is measuring a general personality factor rather than conspiracy belief - it predicted specific beliefs OVER AND ABOVE the other measures · outcome: held
span.quote: Finally, the CMQ predicted beliefs in specific conspiracy theories over and above other individual difference measures.

span.label: whether the samples support the cross-cultural claim
span.note: eliminates: nothing - `our samples were NOT REPRESENTATIVE of the general population of the different countries`, and the between-country comparison is offered as `at least tentative` · outcome: failed
span.quote: First, our samples were not representative of the general population of the different countries, and any generalization should therefore proceed with caution.

span.label: five stated exclusion criteria applied before analysis - repeated submissions from one computer, identical responses to every item, self-reported poor command of the language, more than one missing item, and incomplete conspiracy-mentality data
span.note: eliminates: duplicate participation, straight-lining, comprehension failure and incomplete measurement in an uncontrolled online sample · outcome: held
span.quote: A total of 7,766 volunteers responded to 38 items measuring participants’ belief in conspiracy theories. 1.2% ( n = 93) of the submissions were excluded due to (a) repeated submissions from one computer, (b) identical responses to all items, (c) self-reported poor command of the questionnaire language, or (d) missing responses to more than one questionnaire item.

span.label: back-translating every item by a second bilingual and resolving disagreements by discussion
span.note: eliminates: the possibility that cross-country differences are translation artefacts rather than differences in the construct · outcome: held
span.quote: The original English items were translated into German and Turkish in a procedure similar to that proposed by Brislin ( 1970 ): Each item was first translated by a native speaker of the respective language and then translated back into English by a different person competent in both languages.

span.label: a deliberately broad, non-judgmental definition of conspiracy theory plus an instruction that there are no objectively right or wrong answers
span.note: eliminates: suppression of endorsement by participants who read the question as an accusation of credulity · outcome: held
span.quote: They then received a very broad and non-judgmental definition of the term conspiracy theory : “A conspiracy theory is a theory that provides an alternative explanation to the established understanding of a historical or current event.

span.label: specifying in advance that correlations with neighbouring constructs must exist but must not be high enough to threaten independence
span.note: eliminates: the possibility of declaring success either way - a correlation that is too high would refute the construct rather than support it · outcome: held
span.quote: At the same time, we expect that none of the correlations will reach a level that would cast doubt on the viability of conspiracy mentality as an independent construct.

span.label: conspiracy mentality
span.quote: As such, a conspiracy mentality then describes the general propensity to subscribe to theories blaming a conspiracy of ill-intending individuals or groups for important societal phenomena or, in more abstract terms, the tendency to subscribe to “general conspiracist beliefs”

span.label: conspiracist ideation
span.quote: There have been a number of initial efforts to measure individual differences in conspiracy mentality (sometimes called “conspiracist ideation”; Swami et al., 2011 ), the most prominent of which is Swami and colleagues’ Belief in Conspiracy Theories Inventory

span.label: Conspiracy Mentality Questionnaire
span.quote: In this context, we will propose the Conspiracy Mentality Questionnaire (CMQ), a short (5-item) measure of generic conspiracy beliefs that we administered in a large ( N = 7,766) international study spanning North American (US), Western European (UK and Ireland; Germany), and Middle Eastern (Turkey) cultures

span.label: Generic Conspiracist Beliefs Scale
span.quote: Hitherto, there have been two attempts to address this challenge, however, neither explicitly address the cross-cultural validity of the measurement instruments. First, Brotherton et al. ( in press ) have developed a 15-item Generic Conspiracist Beliefs Scale on the basis of an exploratory factor analysis of 75 items. They were able to differentiate between five major components of generic conspiracy beliefs: governmental conspiracies, extraterrestrial conspiracies, informational control conspiracies, personal well-being conspiracies, and malevolent global conspiracies. These dimensions are also reflected in the final scale.

span.label: Conspiracy Mentality Scale
span.quote: Second, Imhoff and Bruder ( in press ) developed a 12-item Conspiracy Mentality Scale. The items of this instrument not only avoid mentioning any specific alleged conspiracy, but also do not name any specific groups that may be responsible for a conspiracy (example item: “Most people do not recognize to what extent our life is determined by conspiracies that are concocted in secret”)

span.label: Belief in Conspiracy Theories Inventory
span.quote: There have been a number of initial efforts to measure individual differences in conspiracy mentality (sometimes called “conspiracist ideation”; Swami et al., 2011 ), the most prominent of which is Swami and colleagues’ Belief in Conspiracy Theories Inventory

span.label: specific conspiracy theories
span.quote: Individuals differ not only in the degree to which they believe in specific conspiracy theories, but also in their general susceptibility to explanations based on such theories, that is, their conspiracy mentality . We present the Conspiracy Mentality Questionnaire (CMQ), an instrument designed to efficiently assess differences in the generic tendency to engage in conspiracist ideation within and across cultures.

span.label: measurement equivalence
span.quote: Analyses based on a cross-cultural sample (Study 1a; N = 7,766) supported the conceptualization of conspiracy mentality as a one-dimensional construct across the three language versions of the CMQ that is stable across time (Study 1b; N = 141). Multi-group confirmatory factor analysis demonstrated cross-cultural measurement equivalence of the CMQ items.

span.label: discriminant validity
span.quote: At the same time, we expect that none of the correlations will reach a level that would cast doubt on the viability of conspiracy mentality as an independent construct.

span.label: anomia
span.quote: In particular, conspiracy mentality should be positively related to instruments gauging perceptions of low socio-political power (Abalakina-Paap et al., 1999 ) and anomia (Goertzel, 1994 ), paranoia and schizotypy (Grzesiak-Feldman and Ejsmont, 2008 ; Holm, 2009 ), paranormal belief (Ramsay, 2006 ), RWA (Adorno et al., 1950 ), and the personality dimensions of agreeableness (negatively) and openness to experience (positively) (Swami et al., 2010 , 2011 ).

span.label: backtranslated
span.quote: Disagreements between the original and the backtranslated version and their implications for the translated version were resolved by discussion.

span.label: schizotypy
span.quote: Further, in Studies 2–4, we test the convergent and discriminant validity of the construct of conspiracy mentality compared to other generalized political attitudes [right-wing authoritarianism (RWA), social dominance orientation (SDO)], personality measures (Big Five, schizotypy, paranoid ideation), and further individual differences measures (e.g., domains of paranormal belief, power-, and control-related self-perceptions, anomia, death anxiety).

span.label: conspiracy mentality - `the general susceptibility to explanations based on such theories, THAT IS, their conspiracy mentality`, and operationally the CMQ. FOUR NAMES FOR THIS ONE THING appear in a single paragraph, each attributed: conspiracy mentality (Moscovici), CONSPIRACIST IDEATION (Swami), general conspiracist beliefs (Swami), generic conspiracy beliefs (here)
span.quote: There have been a number of initial efforts to measure individual differences in conspiracy mentality (sometimes called “conspiracist ideation”; Swami et al., 2011 ), the most prominent of which is Swami and colleagues’ Belief in Conspiracy Theories Inventory

span.label: and the term has a datable origin the paper gives: `THIS TERM WAS ORIGINALLY PHRASED BY MOSCOVICI (1987)`, for whom a conspiracy was an `indissoluble secret bond` whose object is `to foment upheaval in society, pervert societal values, aggravate crises, promote defeat`
span.quote: This term was originally phrased by Moscovici ( 1987 ) who understood the notion of conspiracy as implying “that members of a confession, party, or ethnicity […] are united by an indissoluble secret bond. The object of such an alliance is to foment upheaval in society, pervert societal values, aggravate crises, promote defeat, and so on.

span.label: FOUR INSTRUMENTS FOR ONE CONSTRUCT, AND THE TWO CALLING THEMSELVES GENERIC DISAGREE ABOUT ITS SHAPE. Brotherton's Generic Conspiracist Beliefs Scale: 15 items, FIVE components. This paper's CMQ: 5 items, ONE dimension. Same journal, same year, same construct name
span.quote: Hitherto, there have been two attempts to address this challenge, however, neither explicitly address the cross-cultural validity of the measurement instruments. First, Brotherton et al. span.quote: However, scales measuring beliefs in specific conspiracy theories are closely bound to specific temporal and geographical contexts. In response to these limitations, it has been suggested that there is a need to assess the general tendency to believe in conspiracies in a way that is not dependent on the cultural familiarity of selected theories (Brotherton, French, and Pickering; in press) and also independent of knowledge about specific conspiracy theories which may vary between cultures.

span.label: conspiracy theory - THE DEFINITION GIVEN TO PARTICIPANTS, deliberately broad and non-judgmental, explicitly leaving the truth question open
